title: Root Canal or Extraction? A Patient's Guide to Deciding
metaTitle: Root Canal or Extraction? A Guide to Deciding
metaDescription: Should you save a tooth with a root canal or have it pulled? Compare keeping your natural tooth versus extraction and replacement, with guidance from Markham.
excerpt: Should you save a tooth with a root canal or have it pulled? This guide weighs keeping your natural tooth against extraction and replacement options.
heroImageAlt: Patient and dentist reviewing an X-ray while deciding between a root canal and an extraction.
bodyHtml:
When a tooth is badly infected or damaged, you are often choosing between a root canal to save it and an extraction to remove it (usually followed by a replacement). In many cases, dentists lean toward saving the natural tooth when it has a reasonable outlook, because nothing fully replaces your own tooth. But the right decision is personal and depends on the condition of the tooth, your health, and your priorities around cost, time, and comfort. This guide lays out the trade-offs so you can discuss them with your dentist.

The case for saving the tooth

A root canal removes the infected pulp and lets you keep the natural tooth, root and all. That matters because a natural tooth helps preserve the surrounding jawbone, keeps neighbouring teeth from drifting, and maintains your natural bite and chewing. Keeping your own tooth also avoids the separate process of replacing it. Root canal treatment has a high success rate, and a well-restored treated tooth can last many years. You can read more about what the procedure involves on the root canal therapy at Smile Dental Arts Centre page.

The case for extraction

Sometimes a tooth is too far gone to save predictably — for instance, if it is cracked deep below the gum, severely broken down, or affected by advanced gum disease and bone loss. In those situations, removing the tooth and replacing it may be the more reliable long-term plan. Extraction resolves the immediate problem, but it is rarely the end of the story: leaving a gap can cause neighbouring teeth to shift and bone to shrink over time, so a replacement is usually recommended.

If a tooth is removed, what replaces it?

Common options include:

  • Dental implant — a titanium post that supports a crown; it does not rely on neighbouring teeth, but treatment can take several months.
  • Fixed bridge — a false tooth anchored to the teeth on either side.
  • Removable partial denture — a removable appliance that fills the gap.

Each has its own benefits, costs, and timelines, which your dentist can outline for your situation. It is worth factoring the replacement into the decision from the start, so you are comparing the full journey of saving the tooth against the full journey of removing and replacing it.

How to weigh it up

A few questions can help frame the decision:

  • How restorable is the tooth? Is there enough healthy structure to rebuild it after a root canal?
  • What is the long-term outlook? A tooth likely to heal is a strong candidate to save; one with a poor prognosis may not be.
  • What does each path involve overall? Saving the tooth is often a shorter journey; extraction plus a replacement such as an implant can involve more stages.
  • What are the costs over time? The lower up-front cost is not always lower in the long run; discuss specifics directly with the clinic.
  • What matters most to you? Keeping a natural tooth, total treatment time, and comfort all carry different weight for different people.

Is a root canal always better than pulling the tooth?

Often it is preferable to keep the natural tooth, but not always — when a tooth's outlook is poor, a planned extraction and replacement can be the healthier choice. The assessment of the individual tooth is what decides it.

Is pulling a tooth cheaper than a root canal?

Extraction may cost less at first, but replacing the tooth afterward adds to the total. Looking at the full picture, rather than the first step alone, gives a fairer comparison.

Does it hurt more to save or to remove a tooth?

Both are done with the area numbed, and most people manage the recovery with routine aftercare. Comfort should not be the only deciding factor; the tooth's prospects matter more.

Deciding with your dentist

Because so much rides on the specific tooth, this is a decision to make with a dentist who can examine it and review your X-rays. Dr. Neda Kadivar, a general and family dentist with over 20 years of experience, can talk through saving versus replacing a tooth with the team at Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham, Ontario.

This article is general information and not a substitute for professional dental advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with a licensed dentist about your specific situation.
